editorial.marketOverview: The next three US sessions (November 23–25) retain a bearish, elevated-downside-risk baseline. Friday's steep QQQ/Nasdaq decline and more severe semiconductor liquidation indicate concentrated AI leadership stress, while volatility and weak breadth argue against treating oversold conditions as an established bottom. No Sunday US cash session exists; weekend headlines do not establish a new market reaction.
editorial.whatChanged: The November 22 week-ahead preview again focuses on Wednesday PCE and GDP, Monday PMI, and Dell/HPE hardware earnings. Asian-market coverage flags foreign selling and semiconductor contagion, already represented in the previous assessment. No new curated Open Watch event or independently verified fresh US price response changes the baseline.
editorial.marketInterpretation: The SOX underperformance versus the Nasdaq and broad Friday decline support a risk-off interpretation. A reflex short-covering rally is plausible after unusually large losses, but durable recovery requires chips and QQQ to rise together with breadth improvement and easing VXN/VIX. Friday Treasury and oil figures cannot be used as contemporaneous cross-asset confirmation.
editorial.threeDayPath: Monday: watch the first synchronized cash-market response, flash PMIs and NVDA/SOX relative strength; a volatile opening rebound may fail without breadth. Tuesday: consumer confidence and hardware earnings may amplify or moderate AI demand concerns. Wednesday: clustered PCE, GDP, durable goods and Beige Book events raise gap and rate-repricing risk. This is a conditional scenario, not a predicted price path.
editorial.bullCase: A sharp oversold bounce becomes more credible if QQQ and SOX/SMH jointly regain ground, breadth turns convincingly positive and VXN/VIX decline. Softer inflation and stable yields could help duration-sensitive technology, but upcoming data and their market impact remain unknown.
editorial.bearCase: Further NVDA/semiconductor weakness, continued negative breadth and elevated volatility would confirm liquidation risk. Hot inflation or hawkish repricing could pressure technology multiples; the direction of the releases and Fed reaction are not known in advance.
